hints: Treat every mine coordinate as a zero; all other cells are ones.
For a candidate center, the plus order is limited by the shortest of its four consecutive-one runs.
Because rows and columns are scanned in both directions, each cell can accumulate its four directional limits without explicitly expanding from every center.
Use one DP matrix and repeatedly take minimums to keep the memory usage at O(n^2).
title: Largest Plus Sign Problem

constraints: All the pairs (x_i, y_i) are unique.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: A zero at the bottom edge limits the vertical arm length; the largest valid axis-aligned plus has order 2.
The only cell is a mine, so there is no cell that can serve as the center of a plus sign.

content.problemStatement:
You receive an integer `n`. You have an `n x n` binary grid `grid` with all values initially `1`'s except for some indices given in the array `mines`. The `i^th` element of the array `mines` is defined as `mines[i] = [x_i, y_i]` where `grid[x_i][y_i] == 0`.

Output *the order of the largest **axis-aligned** plus sign of* 1*'s contained in* `grid`. If there is none, output `0`.

An **axis-aligned plus sign** of `1`'s of order `k` has some center `grid[r][c] == 1` along with four arms of length `k - 1` going up, down, left, and right, and made of `1`'s. Keep in mind that there could be `0`'s or `1`'s beyond the arms of the plus sign, only the relevant area of the plus sign is checked for `1`'s.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/06/13/plus1-grid.jpg)

```
Input: n = 5, mines = [[4,2]]
Output: 2
Explanation: In the above grid, the largest plus sign can only be of order 2. One of them is shown.
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/06/13/plus2-grid.jpg)

```
Input: n = 1, mines = [[0,0]]
Output: 0
Explanation: There is no plus sign, so return 0.
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= n <= 500`
* `1 <= mines.length <= 5000`
* `0 <= x_i, y_i < n`
* All the pairs `(x_i, y_i)` are **unique**.

notes: A mine is treated as a zero cell and breaks every horizontal or vertical run passing through it.
solution.approach: Use dynamic programming over the grid. For each cell, compute the longest consecutive run of available 1-cells ending at that cell from each of the four directions. The minimum of those four directional run lengths is the largest plus-sign order centered at that cell. Take the maximum over all cells.

better.description: Precompute directional consecutive-one counts for rows and columns, then combine them at each cell. Using one DP matrix is enough because each directional pass can immediately take the minimum with previously stored bounds.

optimal.description: Store the minimum horizontal run length in a single DP matrix, then sweep the columns top-to-bottom and bottom-to-top while taking minimums. The resulting dp[r][c] equals the maximum order of a plus centered at (r,c).

bruteForce.complexity: Time O(n^3), auxiliary space O(n^2) for the blocked grid.
bruteForce.description: Try every non-mine cell as a center and expand the four arms one layer at a time until a boundary or mine is reached. This directly follows the definition but can take O(n^3) time in the worst case.

followUps: Can the same O(n^2) time solution be implemented with less than O(n^2) auxiliary space?
How would the solution change if mines could be added or removed between queries?
What implementation changes are needed if n is much larger and the grid cannot fit in memory?
